about: The scripted AI lesson for p1-heating (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p1-energy-stores and p1-power.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about heating: why some things need far more energy to warm up than others, and how to work out the energy needed.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. A kettle heats some water. Which store of the water rises?
steps.right: Yes: the water gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.

wrong.other: Not quite: its thermal store, because the water gets hotter.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: the water stays in the kettle. It gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.
wrong.chemical: Not quite: water is not a fuel. It gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.

idk.hint: The water gets hotter. Which store depends on how hot something is?

steps.answerWhy: The water gets hotter, so its thermal store rises.

steps.question: Second: a 2 kW heater is on for 10 s. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?

wrong.nokw: Not quite: 20 000 J. Change kilowatts to watts first: 2 kW = 2000 W. Then 2000 × 10 = 20 000 J.

idk.hint: 2 kW is 2000 W. Multiply that by the 10 s.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Heat 1 kg of water and 1 kg of cooking oil in two pans on the same hob: the oil gets hot about twice as fast. Different materials need different amounts of energy to warm up by the same amount.

Temperature tells you how hot or cold something is, in degrees Celsius (°C). When something is heated, its rise in temperature depends on its mass in kilograms (kg), what it is made of, and how much energy goes in.
The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1 °C is called its specific heat capacity, c. Its unit is joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg °C).
Water has a high specific heat capacity: 4200 J/kg °C. It takes 4200 J to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C. Most metals need far less: copper needs only about 390 J.

steps.question: 1 kg of water and 1 kg of copper are each given 4200 J. Which one gets hotter?
steps.right: Yes: copper needs only about 390 J for each degree, so 4200 J warms it by about 11 °C. The water warms by only 1 °C.

wrong.other: Not quite: the copper. It needs far less energy for each degree, so the same energy warms it much more.
wrong.water: Not quite: water needs 4200 J for each degree, so it warms by only 1 °C. Copper needs about 390 J for each degree, so it warms by about 11 °C.
wrong.same: Not quite: only the water warms by 1 °C. Copper needs about 390 J for each degree, so 4200 J warms it by about 11 °C.

idk.hint: Copper needs much less energy for each degree than water does. So with the same energy, which warms more?

steps.answerWhy: Copper needs far less energy for each degree, so the same 4200 J warms it about 11 °C, and the water only 1 °C.

steps.text: The Greek letter Δ, delta, means "change in". Δθ, said "delta theta", is the change in temperature: the final temperature minus the starting temperature.

The equation is ΔE = m c Δθ: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change. ΔE is in joules (J), m is the mass in kilograms (kg), c is the specific heat capacity in J/kg °C and Δθ is the temperature change in °C.

steps.question: Water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. What is Δθ?

wrong.final: Not quite: 70 °C is the final temperature. Δθ is the change: 70 − 20 = 50 °C.
wrong.added: Not quite: take the start away, do not add it. Δθ = 70 − 20 = 50 °C.

idk.hint: Δθ is the change: take the starting temperature away from the final one.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is specific heat capacity?
points: the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1 °C
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1 °C.

steps.text: Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: How much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C? (c = 4200 J/kg °C)
steps: Write the equation: ΔE = m c Δθ.

steps.question: Your turn. How much energy is needed to heat 0.5 kg of water from 10 °C to 30 °C, in joules? (c = 4200 J/kg °C)

wrong.final: Not quite: 42 000 J. 30 °C is the final temperature. Use the change: Δθ = 30 − 10 = 20 °C, so ΔE = 0.5 × 4200 × 20 = 42 000 J.
wrong.start: Not quite: 42 000 J. 10 °C is the starting temperature. Use the change: Δθ = 30 − 10 = 20 °C, so ΔE = 0.5 × 4200 × 20 = 42 000 J.

steps.text: Masses given in grams must be changed to kilograms first: divide by 1000. 250 g is 0.25 kg.

steps.question: A 200 g block of aluminium is warmed by 10 °C. c = 900 J/kg °C. How much energy does it take in, in joules?

wrong.grams: Not quite: 1800 J. The mass must be in kilograms: 200 g = 0.2 kg. Then ΔE = 0.2 × 900 × 10 = 1800 J.

idk.hint: Change 200 g to kilograms by dividing by 1000. Then multiply by 900 and by 10.

steps.text: Cooling works the same way, but energy is given out. A 1.5 kg aluminium block cooling from 80 °C to 20 °C gives out 1.5 × 900 × 60 = 81 000 J.
To find c, Δθ or m, put the numbers in first, then divide. On a calculator, put the bottom of the division in brackets: 15 000 ÷ (5 × 10), not 15 000 ÷ 5 × 10.

steps.question: 5 kg of a material takes in 15 000 J, and its temperature rises by 10 °C. What is its specific heat capacity, in J/kg °C?

wrong.brackets: Not quite: 300 J/kg °C. Put the bottom in brackets: 15 000 ÷ (5 × 10) = 15 000 ÷ 50 = 300. Without brackets the calculator multiplies by 10 instead.
wrong.times: Not quite: 300 J/kg °C. To find c, divide: c = 15 000 ÷ (5 × 10) = 300 J/kg °C.

idk.hint: Work out 5 × 10 first, which is 50. Then divide 15 000 by 50.

steps.question: 2 kg of water is given 84 000 J. c = 4200 J/kg °C. How much does its temperature rise, in °C?

wrong.nomass: Not quite: 10 °C. Divide by the mass as well: Δθ = 84 000 ÷ (2 × 4200) = 84 000 ÷ 8400 = 10 °C.

idk.hint: Work out 2 × 4200 first. Then divide 84 000 by it.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the most common mistake with Δθ, and how do you avoid it?
points: using a temperature instead of the change in temperature
take the start from the final temperature first
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: people use the final temperature instead of the change; always work out final minus start first.

keyPoints.heading: Required practical — measuring specific heat capacity

steps.text: Next, a required practical: one you could be asked about in the exam. The aim is to measure the specific heat capacity of a material, such as a metal block or some water.
A heater goes into one hole in a metal block, and a thermometer into another. The heater is wired to a joulemeter, a meter that measures the energy supplied in joules.
Measure the mass of the block and its starting temperature. Switch on the heater, and after a set time read the energy on the joulemeter and the new temperature. Then c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ).

steps.question: At the end, why should you wait a little before reading the thermometer?

options.text: So the thermometer reaches the block's temperature
So the block cools to room temperature

steps.right: Yes: the thermometer takes time to warm up to the temperature of the block, so an early reading is too low.

wrong.other: Not quite. You wait so the thermometer reaches the temperature of the block.
wrong.room: Not quite: you want the block's temperature, not room temperature. You wait so the thermometer has time to reach the temperature of the block.
wrong.meter: Not quite: the joulemeter keeps its reading. You wait so the thermometer has time to reach the temperature of the block.

idk.hint: A thermometer does not change its reading instantly. What is it trying to catch up with?

steps.answerWhy: The thermometer needs time to reach the temperature of the block, so an early reading is too low.

steps.text: The main problem is that some energy escapes from the block to the surroundings. Less energy goes into the block than the joulemeter shows, so its temperature rises less.

steps.question: Energy escaping to the surroundings makes the temperature rise smaller. What does that do to the specific heat capacity you work out?

options.text: It comes out higher than the true value
It comes out lower than the true value

steps.right: Yes: c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). A smaller Δθ on the bottom gives a bigger answer, so c comes out too high.

wrong.other: Not quite: higher than the true value. A smaller Δθ on the bottom of c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ) gives a bigger answer.
wrong.lower: Not quite: Δθ is on the bottom of c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). A smaller number on the bottom gives a bigger answer, so c comes out too high.
wrong.none: Not quite: Δθ is smaller than it should be, and it is on the bottom of c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). That makes c come out too high.

idk.hint: Δθ is on the bottom of c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). Dividing by a smaller number gives a bigger or smaller answer?

steps.answerWhy: Δθ is on the bottom of c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ), so a smaller Δθ makes c come out too high.

steps.text: To reduce the problem, wrap the block in insulation. For water, use an insulated cup with a lid, and stir so the water is the same temperature all through.
If you are asked for a hazard, name the hot heater, block or water, which could burn you. "Electric shock" on its own does not score.
To compare your result with the true value, work out the percentage difference: (your value − true value) ÷ true value × 100.

steps.question: Suppose your result for water is 4410 J/kg °C, and the true value is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the percentage difference?

wrong.base: Not quite: 5%. Divide by the true value, 4200, not by 4410: 210 ÷ 4200 × 100 = 5%.
wrong.ratio: Not quite: 5%. Take the difference first: 4410 − 4200 = 210. Then 210 ÷ 4200 × 100 = 5%.

idk.hint: First the difference: 4410 − 4200. Then divide by the true value, 4200, and multiply by 100.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does the measured specific heat capacity usually come out too high, and how can you reduce that?
points: insulate the block (or use a lid)
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: some energy escapes to the surroundings, so the temperature rises less; insulating the block reduces that.

steps.text: Last part: what heating does inside a material. Everything is made of tiny particles that are always moving. Heating something gives its particles more energy.
The total energy of all the particles in a system, from their movement and from the forces between them, is called its internal energy. Heating something raises its internal energy.
Temperature is linked to how fast the particles move on average: the higher the temperature, the more kinetic energy each particle has on average.

steps.question: A big cold lake and a tiny hot spark. Which has more internal energy?

options.text: The lake: it has vastly more particles

steps.right: Yes. Each particle in the spark has more energy on average, but the lake has so many more particles that its total is far bigger.

wrong.other: Not quite: the lake. Internal energy is a total, and the lake has vastly more particles.
wrong.hotter: Not quite: the spark has a higher temperature, so each of its particles has more energy on average. But internal energy is the total for all the particles, and the lake has vastly more.
wrong.same: Not quite: internal energy is the total for all the particles, and the lake has vastly more of them, so the lake has more.

idk.hint: Internal energy is the total for all the particles. Which has far more particles?

steps.answerWhy: Internal energy is a total, and the lake has vastly more particles than the spark.

steps.text: Water's high specific heat capacity makes it useful. Central heating uses water because each kilogram carries a lot of energy to the radiators. And places by the sea have milder weather, because the sea warms up and cools down slowly.

steps.question: A car engine is cooled by water pumped around it. Why is water a good choice?

options.text: It can take in a lot of energy without getting very hot

steps.right: Yes: water's high specific heat capacity means it can take in a lot of energy from the engine while its own temperature rises only a little.

wrong.other: Not quite. Water can take in a lot of energy without getting very hot, because of its high specific heat capacity.
wrong.quick: Not quite: the other way round. Water warms up slowly, because it needs a lot of energy for each degree. That lets it take in a lot of energy from the engine.
wrong.stops: Not quite: water carries energy away from the engine. Its high specific heat capacity means it takes in a lot without getting very hot.

idk.hint: Water needs a lot of energy for each degree it warms. Is that good for soaking up energy from an engine?

steps.answerWhy: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it takes in a lot of energy while warming only a little.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the difference between temperature and internal energy?
points: temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles
internal energy is the total energy of all the particles
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles, but internal energy is the total energy of all of them.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: water is heated from 15 °C to 40 °C. What is Δθ, in °C?
Quiz, question 2 of 6: how much energy warms 1 kg of water by 5 °C, in joules? (c = 4200 J/kg °C)

wrong.other: Not quite: 21 000 J. ΔE = m c Δθ = 1 × 4200 × 5 = 21 000 J.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: what is specific heat capacity?

options.text: The energy needed to raise 1 kg of a material by 1 °C
The temperature at which a material boils
How fast energy passes through a material

steps.right: Yes: the energy needed to raise 1 kg by 1 °C.

wrong.other: Not quite: it is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a material by 1 °C.

steps.answerWhy: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: 2 kg of oil (c = 2000 J/kg °C) takes in 40 000 J. How much does its temperature rise, in °C?
Quiz, question 5 of 6: in the practical, why is the block wrapped in insulation?

options.text: To reduce the energy escaping to the surroundings
To make the heater more powerful
To keep the mass of the block the same

steps.right: Yes: less energy escapes, so the result is closer to the true value.

wrong.other: Not quite: insulation reduces the energy escaping to the surroundings, so the result is closer to the true value.

steps.answerWhy: Insulation reduces the energy escaping to the surroundings.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: temperature is linked to…

options.text: …the average kinetic energy of the particles

steps.right: Yes: the higher the temperature, the more kinetic energy each particle has on average.

wrong.other: Not quite: temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles.

steps.answerWhy: Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles.
